name: 味の天徳 京都四条木屋町店 (Aji no Tentoku Kyoto Shijo Kiyamachi)

claims.text: Core dish is wheat abura soba noodles dressed in a soy-based tare; no gluten-free option or allergen separation indicated anywhere.
The abura soba uses a 醤油ベース (soy-sauce-based) tare; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.
Standard bowl is topped with chashu (pork); no vegan/vegetarian preparation is advertised.
Uses plant-based (vegetable) oil rather than animal fat in the dressing — a lighter-fat bowl, though this does not make it gluten-free or vegan.
The shoyu tonkotsu bowl uses a soy-sauce-based tare, which in Japanese ramen almost always contains wheat; the miso bowl likewise sits on wheat noodles and pork broth.
All ramen is built on pork-bone broth with back fat and chashu; broth and noodles share the same single-operator kitchen, so there is no vegan-safe preparation.
The ramen is a tonkotsu-shoyu (soy-sauce based) style; soy-sauce tare in Japanese ramen almost always contains wheat, on top of the wheat-flour noodles themselves.
Broth is pork-bone and chicken-carcass based with pork chashu and animal toppings throughout; no separate vegetable/vegan preparation is indicated.

name: 中国料理 くれたけ (Chugoku Ryori Kuretake)

claims.text: Noodles are wheat and the broths use soy sauce (wheat shoyu) plus a sesame base; the kitchen is a general town-Chinese kitchen making gyoza, fried rice and stir-fries, so wheat and soy are pervasive. No gluten-free handling is documented.
The sake-lees ramen is explicitly a soy-sauce ramen (醤油ラーメン) with sake lees dissolved in, indicating standard wheat-containing soy sauce in the tare.
Signature bowls use chicken/pork/vegetable broth and char siu, and the tantanmen is topped with minced-meat miso; no vegan preparation is documented.

name: 中国料理 菜格 (Chugoku Ryori Saikaku)

claims.text: Wheat noodles, wheat dumpling skins, and wheat-containing Chinese seasonings (soy/bean pastes) are central to the menu and share a single one-cook wok station; assume heavy gluten cross-contact.
Sichuan dishes such as the mapo tofu and the chili/sesame tantanmen tare rely on soy- and fermented-bean-based seasonings that typically contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is indicated.
Signature dishes use pork and animal-based broth/condiments throughout; no dedicated plant-based prep is indicated, and a single chef cooks everything in shared woks.
Tiny 14-seat counter with one attentive chef-owner who takes reservations, so allergy questions can be raised directly when booking — though no formal allergen handling is documented.

name: 中華のサカイ 本店 (Chuka no Sakai Honten)

claims.text: The chuka-soba is a traditional soy-based Chinese noodle soup; soy sauce in this style of cooking is conventionally wheat-based, though the shop publishes no specific allergen details.
The kitchen is a meat-and-fish Chinese kitchen and the signature cold noodles are topped with roast pork, so cross-contact with animal products is pervasive.
Wheat ramen noodles are boiled and animal/soy-based broth, gyoza and karaage are prepared in the same small kitchen, so heavy wheat cross-contact is unavoidable for a celiac.
The chuka-soba broth is built on a soy-sauce (醤油) base, which in a town-Chinese kitchen is standard wheat-containing soy sauce.
Menu is meat- and seafood-centered (char siu, fried chicken, shrimp dumplings, crab omelette, pork trotters) with shared woks; vegetable dishes likely use animal-based seasonings.

name: 中華料理 大鵬 (Chuka Ryori Taiho)

claims.text: Wheat-based noodles (ramen, chuka-soba, dan-dan, hot-and-sour noodles) and wheat-wrapped dumplings/dim sum are core to the menu, with heavy use of wheat soy sauce and Chinese sauces in a shared wok kitchen - high gluten exposure throughout.
Chinese-style cooking with soy and bean-paste seasonings; standard wheat-containing soy sauce should be assumed. No wheat-free tare or sauce is documented.
Menu is built on pork, wagyu, chicken and seafood, with meat/seafood broths and shared woks; vegetable dishes are very likely cooked with animal fats and meat-based seasonings.
